readings.title: Mrs. Redwing’s Speckled Egg
readings.challenge: Keep track of two things the Breezes do all morning: teasing and helping.
readings.focus: Playful mischief becomes a rescue when the Breezes use their tricks for someone in trouble.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Mrs. Redwing is a red-winged blackbird. Bulrushes are tall plants that grow in wet ground. On a farm a breakfast horn was blown to call people in to eat.
readings.contentNote: Farmer Brown hunts Johnny Chuck with a gun, and a boy sets out to take a bird’s eggs. Neither of them succeeds.

excerpt.locator: Chapter I, “Mrs. Redwing’s Speckled Egg,” the whole chapter; opens “OLD MOTHER WEST WIND came down from the Purple Hills in the golden light of the early…”; closes “…knew, that some day out of that pretty new speckled egg would come a wee baby Redwing.”.

questions.prompt: What do the Breezes do to Johnny Chuck at breakfast? Does he really mind?
facilitatorNotes: They snatch his corn leaf, pull his whiskers and rumple his hair. He pretends to be cross, but he loves them, and they warn him when Farmer Brown comes.
evidence: Johnny Chuck pretended to be very cross indeed, but really he didn’t mind a bit

questions.prompt: How do the Breezes keep Tommy Brown away from the nest? Retell the chase.
facilitatorNotes: They take turns blowing his straw hat away just as he reaches it, all the way across the meadow and the brook, and hang it in a thorn tree. By then he has forgotten the nest, and the breakfast horn calls him home.
evidence: Then they took turns
they hung the old straw hat in the middle of a thorn tree

questions.prompt: Why does Tommy Brown want the eggs? What do you think of his reason?
facilitatorNotes: “Just because they were pretty,” not because he needs them. Ask whether liking something is a reason to take it. Some children may say he does not understand that eggs hold baby birds.
evidence: just because they were pretty

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs. Redwing sing for joy at the end? What do she and the Breezes both know?
facilitatorNotes: That a baby Redwing will hatch from the speckled egg. They saved more than a pretty egg; they saved a bird to come.
evidence: some day out of that pretty new speckled egg would come a wee baby Redwing

readings.title: Why Grandfather Frog Has No Tail
readings.challenge: Hear a story told inside another story, and notice who is listening to it.
readings.focus: A made-up “why” story wraps around something true: tadpoles lose their tails as they grow into frogs.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Pollywogs, also called tadpoles, are baby frogs that live in water and have tails. Grandfather Frog’s tale of the proud King Frog is invented, but the change from tadpole to frog is real. To be vain is to be too proud of how you look.

excerpt.locator: Chapter II, “Why Grandfather Frog Has No Tail,” the whole chapter; opens “OLD MOTHER WEST WIND had gone to her day’s work, leaving all the Merry Little Breezes to…”; closes “…first and tell him that Farmer Brown was coming down on the Green Meadows with a gun.”.

questions.prompt: How can the Pollywogs be Grandfather Frog’s grandchildren when they look nothing like him?
facilitatorNotes: They are tadpoles, and tadpoles grow into frogs. The story says you would never guess unless someone told you.
evidence: They didn’t look the least bit like Grandfather Frog.

questions.prompt: When Grandfather Frog mentions hungry Mink, Billy Mink squirms and looks away. Why?
facilitatorNotes: Minks eat young frogs, and Billy feels caught. Grandfather Frog makes his point right in front of him.
evidence: squirmed uneasily and looked away guiltily

questions.prompt: What did the King Frog do all day, and why did Mother Nature take his tail?
facilitatorNotes: He ate, slept and admired his tail, and soon all the Frogs copied him. She took the thing he was vain about.
evidence: He did nothing at all but eat and sleep and admire his tail.

questions.prompt: Grandfather Frog says that people who do nothing worth while are “of no use.” Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: The story is hard on the Frogs. Some children will say everyone matters, even when resting or playing; others will say the Frogs’ real fault was thinking only of themselves. Both views can point to the words.
evidence: people who do nothing worth while in this world are of no use and there is little room for them

readings.title: How Reddy Fox Was Surprised
readings.challenge: Follow Johnny Chuck’s feelings as they change: lost, frightened, furious, then pleased.
readings.focus: A small animal’s sudden anger turns a bully’s trick around.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Johnny Chuck is a woodchuck, a plump animal that lives in a burrow. Bowser is a farm hound, a hunting dog. A “’fraid-cat” is a teasing name for someone who is scared.

excerpt.locator: Chapter III, “How Reddy Fox Was Surprised,” the whole chapter; opens “JOHNNY CHUCK and Reddy Fox lived very near together on the edge of the Green Meadows.…”; closes “And this is the way that Reddy Fox was surprised and that Johnny Chuck found his way home.”.

questions.prompt: What had Johnny Chuck’s mother told him, and what did he do?
facilitatorNotes: Never to go out of sight of the door. He forgot and kept walking after patches that only looked like clover.
evidence: his mother had told him never to go out of sight of the door

questions.prompt: Johnny thinks he can’t be lost while Mr. Sun winks at him. Why doesn’t that work?
facilitatorNotes: The sun keeps moving across the sky and cannot show the way home; and Johnny falls asleep anyway. Accept either reason.
evidence: So long as I can see great round, red Mr. Sun and he winks at me I can’t be lost

questions.prompt: Reddy Fox expected Johnny to run. What does Johnny do instead, and how does he look?
facilitatorNotes: He chases Reddy, chattering, with every hair standing up so that he looks twice his size.
evidence: so that he seemed twice as big as he really was

questions.prompt: The last line says this is how Johnny Chuck found his way home. How did chasing Reddy get him there?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy ran straight home and passed Johnny’s house on the way, so Johnny followed him back without knowing it.
evidence: going home he passed the house of Johnny Chuck

readings.title: Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes — the broken eggs
readings.challenge: Collect clues the way a detective would, before anyone says who did it.
readings.focus: A mystery begins: someone has broken Mrs. Grouse’s eggs in the night, and Peter Rabbit looks closely.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. This is an invented “why” story; real skunks are simply born striped. Mrs. Ruffed Grouse is a woodland bird that nests on the ground. Buff is a pale yellow-brown. Old Dame Nature rules over the meadow folk in these stories.
readings.contentNote: A mother bird’s eggs are broken and eaten in the night. She is frightened but escapes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes,” from the start to the meadow folk gathering at the Great Pine; opens “JIMMY SKUNK, as everybody knows, wears a striped suit, a suit of black and white. There…”; closes “…Mrs. Ruffed Grouse sat beside her empty nest, with all the broken shells about her.”.

questions.prompt: Long ago in this story, why could no one prove who did mischief at night?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmy Skunk’s coat was all black, so he could not be seen in the dark. Keep this clue for tomorrow.
evidence: his coat was so black that in the darkness of the night it was not visible at all

questions.prompt: What does Peter Rabbit do after he hears Mrs. Grouse’s story?
facilitatorNotes: He searches the ground carefully, behind the tree and under the bushes, and then whispers what he found to Johnny Chuck.
evidence: Peter Rabbit looked the ground over very carefully.

questions.prompt: How does Jimmy Skunk act when Peter and Johnny come to his house? Does anything seem odd?
facilitatorNotes: He is in bed in the morning, sleepy and cross, says “Too bad!” with a yawn, and has “other business.” Some children will already suspect him; others will not yet. Both are fair at this point.
evidence: said Jimmy Skunk, and yawned sleepily
he had some other business that morning

questions.prompt: Who do you think broke the eggs? Which clue makes you think so?
facilitatorNotes: A prediction: accept any guess that names a clue from the story, and come back to it tomorrow.
evidence: Jimmy Skunk was in bed. He was very sleepy and very cross

readings.title: Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes — the meeting at the Great Pine
readings.challenge: Put the clues together, the way Old Dame Nature does, to reach an answer.
readings.focus: Questions and evidence, not guessing, uncover the egg thief, and his punishment fits the way he hid.
readings.context: Recap: someone broke and ate Mrs. Grouse’s eggs in the night. Peter Rabbit searched the ground, and Jimmy Skunk was strangely sleepy that morning. Now Old Dame Nature has called all the meadow folk to the Great Pine. A culprit is the one who did a wrong thing; to accuse is to say someone did it; descendants are children, grandchildren and so on.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “Why Jimmy Skunk Wears Stripes,” from the arrival of the meadow folk to the end of the chapter; opens “Reddy Fox, Peter Rabbit, Johnny Chuck, Billy Mink, Little Joe Otter, Jerry Muskrat, Hooty…”; closes “And this is why that to this day Jimmy Skunk wears a striped suit of black and white.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jimmy Skunk say and do when he arrives at the meeting? Why might he act this way?
facilitatorNotes: He looks sorry, tells Mrs. Grouse how bad he feels, and loudly demands that the culprit be punished. A guilty animal might act extra innocent.
evidence: he loudly demanded that the culprit should be found out and severely punished

questions.prompt: Name the clues. What does each one point to?
facilitatorNotes: Three long black hairs point to a black coat; yellow whiskers to egg yolk; sleepiness to being out all night; and Mother West Wind saw a black shadow going toward Jimmy’s house.
evidence: three long black hairs
It might be the yolk of an egg
People who have been out all night

questions.prompt: Why does Old Dame Nature ask everyone questions instead of just saying who did it?
facilitatorNotes: So everyone hears the evidence and works it out together. Some children may say she wanted to give Jimmy a chance to speak; she does ask him for his answer.
evidence: What have you to say for yourself?

questions.prompt: Why are stripes the right punishment for Jimmy Skunk, in this story?
facilitatorNotes: His black coat hid him at night; a striped coat is always seen and marks him as untrusted. Some children will find it unfair that his descendants must wear stripes too. That is worth talking about.
evidence: that when you move about in the night you will always be visible
henceforth you and your descendants shall wear a striped coat

readings.title: Peter Rabbit Plays a Joke
readings.challenge: Follow the joke as it passes along: who plans it, who it lands on, and who has to run.
readings.focus: A trick meant for one friend lands on a sleeping fox, and the trickster is the one who gets chased.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Happy Jack Squirrel is a gray squirrel who lives in the trees. A mossy log is a fallen tree trunk covered with soft green moss. Real woodchucks like Johnny Chuck have short legs and are good diggers, not jumpers.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Peter Rabbit Plays a Joke,” the whole chapter; opens “ONE morning when big round Mr. Sun was climbing up in the sky and Old Mother West Wind…”; closes “…West Wind were still playing, till he was safe in his own snug little home once more.”.

questions.prompt: What hits Johnny Chuck, first on the head and then on the nose? What do he and Happy Jack do about it?
facilitatorNotes: Nuts dropped by Happy Jack Squirrel. Johnny tumbles off the log, and then both of them laugh, because it was such a good joke. Nobody is hurt or cross.
evidence: He was just in time to see Happy Jack Squirrel drop a nut.
Then they both laughed together, it was such a good joke.

questions.prompt: What has Peter Rabbit really found on the other side of the mossy log? Which of his actions tell you he knows?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy Fox, asleep. Peter tiptoes, whispers, tells Johnny to make no noise, and jumps first, then turns around to watch Johnny. Some children will think Peter did not know the fox was there; ask why he wanted Johnny so quiet.
evidence: you must be very, very still, and not make the least little bit of noise
Then he turned around and sat up to see Johnny Chuck jump

questions.prompt: Johnny Chuck lands right on Reddy Fox. Why does Reddy chase Peter and not Johnny?
facilitatorNotes: When Reddy wakes, the first thing he sees is Peter laughing and holding his sides, and Johnny has rolled behind a bush and lies still. So Reddy thinks Peter jumped on him.
evidence: He thought that Peter Rabbit had jumped on him.
there he lay very, very still

questions.prompt: The chapter is called “Peter Rabbit Plays a Joke.” In the end, who is the joke on? Tell why.
facilitatorNotes: A good answer: on Peter, who has to run for his life and hide in Jimmy Skunk’s house while Johnny walks home safe and tidy. Some children will say it is on Reddy Fox, who is woken up and catches nobody. Both fit the story.
evidence: for Peter Rabbit was very much afraid of Reddy Fox
Johnny Chuck stood up and brushed his little coat very clean

readings.title: How Sammy Jay Was Found Out — the stolen nuts
readings.challenge: Notice the difference between what Sammy Jay shows everyone and what he really does.
readings.focus: A thief hides behind fine manners, but the wind sees more than he thinks.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Sammy Jay is a blue jay, a noisy blue-and-white bird with a crest like a high cap. Happy Jack Squirrel keeps nuts for the winter in a hollow, a hole inside a tree. An idle fellow is someone who does no useful work.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “How Sammy Jay Was Found Out,” from the start to everyone feeling sorry for Happy Jack; opens “SAMMY JAY was very busy, very busy indeed. When anyone happened that way Sammy Jay…”; closes “…tree. And because everyone liked Happy Jack, everyone felt very sorry indeed for him.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Sammy Jay pretend to be doing nothing whenever anyone comes along?
facilitatorNotes: Because he is up to mischief: he is stealing Happy Jack’s nuts and does not want to be seen. Idle people, the story says, almost always get into mischief.
evidence: that is why he pretended to be doing nothing when he thought anyone was looking

questions.prompt: How does Old Mother West Wind find out what Sammy Jay is doing?
facilitatorNotes: She sends one Merry Little Breeze, who dances over the treetops as if he were only playing. Sammy is watching her and the other Breezes, so he never notices this one.
evidence: Sammy Jay, watching Old Mother West Wind and the other Merry Little Breezes, didn’t see this Merry Little Breeze at all

questions.prompt: Sammy Jay says the doctor told him to take a bath in the dew. Old Mother West Wind says nothing. What does each of them know?
facilitatorNotes: Sammy is telling a polite lie to explain why he is out so early. She already knows the truth from the Breeze. Children may guess she is saving it for the right moment; that is worth checking in the next part.
evidence: The doctor has ordered me to take a bath in the dew at sunrise every morning.
Old Mother West Wind said nothing

questions.prompt: Sammy Jay offers to help Happy Jack catch the thief. Why would the thief himself do that?
facilitatorNotes: To look as if he could not possibly be the thief, and perhaps to know what everyone finds out. The words “pretended to feel very badly” show his sorrow is not real.
evidence: Sammy Jay pretended to feel very badly indeed

readings.title: How Sammy Jay Was Found Out — the committee of the whole
readings.challenge: Watch how Old Mother West Wind proves what she knows without saying who did it.
readings.focus: A clever test lets the hidden nuts tell the truth, and a made-up “why” ending explains a real bird’s cry.
readings.context: Recap: Sammy Jay stole Happy Jack Squirrel’s nuts and hid them in an old crow’s nest in the Great Pine, then pretended to help look for the thief. Old Mother West Wind saw it all through one of her Breezes. A committee of the whole is a meeting where everyone comes to decide something together.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “How Sammy Jay Was Found Out,” from the meeting at the Great Pine to the end of the chapter; opens “The next morning all the Merry Little Breezes of Old Mother West Wind were turned out of…”; closes “…that day, Sammy Jay, whenever he tries to call, just screams: “Thief!” “Thief!” “Thief!””.

questions.prompt: Old Mother West Wind asks Sammy Jay whether the nest is his and whether she may take a stick from it. Why does he say yes?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks she will take a stick from the top, where there are no nuts, so he can be polite and lose nothing.
evidence: She will only take one from the top and that won’t matter.

questions.prompt: Where does her stick come from, and what tumbles out after it? Say Happy Jack’s words the way he says them.
facilitatorNotes: She blows a stick out of the bottom of the nest, and down fall hickory nuts, chestnuts, acorns and hazel nuts. Let the child try “Why! Why-e-e!” as a long, amazed cry.
evidence: she blew a big stick right out of the bottom of the old nest
Why! Why-e-e!

questions.prompt: Everyone turns to look at Sammy Jay. What does he do, and what does that tell everyone?
facilitatorNotes: He flies away as fast as he can and will not stop. Running away shows he is the thief, even though no one has said so.
evidence: he was flying off through the wood as fast as he could go

questions.prompt: Real blue jays have a loud, harsh call. Why do you think the storyteller made up this reason for it?
facilitatorNotes: It is a “why” story: the jay must call out the word for what he did, forever. Some children will find that a fair punishment; others will just enjoy hearing a real bird’s cry explained. Try the call together.
evidence: Sammy Jay, whenever he tries to call, just screams

readings.title: Bobby Coon and Reddy Fox Play Tricks — a stone in the doorway
readings.challenge: Picture the meadow at night and keep track of who is awake.
readings.focus: Two night prowlers play a trick on a sleeping friend while a third watches and says nothing.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Bobby Coon is a raccoon, an animal that comes out at night. Boomer the Night Hawk and Mr. Whip-poor-will are birds that call in the dark. Johnny Chuck sleeps in a burrow, a house dug under the ground, with one doorway.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Bobby Coon and Reddy Fox Play Tricks,” from the start to Reddy Fox and Bobby Coon running off to the Laughing Brook; opens “IT was night. All the little stars were looking down and twinkling and twinkling. Mother…”; closes “…going to wake old Grandfather Frog from a nice comfortable sleep on his green lily pad.”.

questions.prompt: How does the storyteller show us that the night is very still? Who is still awake?
facilitatorNotes: Stars twinkle, Mother Moon shines, and every bird is asleep except Hooty the Owl, Boomer the Night Hawk and Mr. Whip-poor-will; even the Breezes sleep. It is so still that Bobby Coon talks to himself.
evidence: It was oh, so still!
began to talk to himself

questions.prompt: Bobby Coon starts to say something about Reddy Fox and stops. Why?
facilitatorNotes: Reddy Fox is right behind him and warns him. Bobby was probably about to say something unkind; children can guess what.
evidence: Be careful what you say about Reddy Fox

questions.prompt: What is the “surprise” Reddy Fox thinks of for Johnny Chuck? Is it really a surprise, or something else?
facilitatorNotes: Rolling a big stone over Johnny’s doorway so he must dig his way out in the morning. It is a trick, and not a kind one; some children may think it is only funny.
evidence: Let’s roll that big stone right over Johnny Chuck’s doorway; then he’ll have to dig his way out in the morning.

questions.prompt: Jimmy Skunk pretends not to see what the others are doing. What do you think he will do next?
facilitatorNotes: A prediction: accept any guess and check it in the next part. Some children will say he is staying out of trouble; others that he is planning something.
evidence: Jimmy Skunk pretended not to see what they were doing.

readings.title: Bobby Coon and Reddy Fox Play Tricks — the tricks come home
readings.challenge: Keep track of three tricks and where each one ends up.
readings.focus: Jimmy Skunk helps a friend and sends the tricksters’ trick back to them.
readings.context: Recap: on a still night, Bobby Coon and Reddy Fox rolled a big stone over the door of Johnny Chuck’s house while he slept, as a trick. Jimmy Skunk pretended not to see, and the two tricksters ran off to wake Grandfather Frog.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “Bobby Coon and Reddy Fox Play Tricks,” from Jimmy Skunk staying behind to the end of the chapter; opens “But Jimmy Skunk didn’t go. He watched Reddy Fox and Bobby Coon until they were nearly to…”; closes “…very hard as he peeped over the hill at Reddy Fox and Bobby Coon, and he won’t tell why.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jimmy Skunk finally get sleepy Johnny Chuck to come up to his door?
facilitatorNotes: He calls three times, and then says he has a surprise. Johnny cannot resist finding out what it is.
evidence: When Johnny Chuck heard that Jimmy Skunk had a surprise for him he wanted to know right away what it could be

questions.prompt: When Johnny Chuck finds the stone, whom does he blame at first? Why does that make sense?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmy Skunk, because Jimmy is the one at his door talking about a surprise. Jimmy tells him who really did it.
evidence: He thought Jimmy Skunk had played him a mean trick

questions.prompt: Where does the big stone end up? And what happens at Bobby Coon’s hollow tree?
facilitatorNotes: Over Reddy Fox’s doorway; and Hooty the Owl stuffs Bobby Coon’s house with sticks and leaves that Jimmy gathers. Each trickster gets a trick like the one he played.
evidence: it filled his doorway
We’ll fill his house full of sticks and leaves

questions.prompt: The storyteller says, “I’m sure I don’t know” what Reddy Fox and Bobby Coon said. Why leave it out? What do you think they said?
facilitatorNotes: So we can imagine their faces and words ourselves, while Mr. Sun laughs. Ask, too, whether Jimmy was being a good friend or just playing tricks of his own; both views can be argued.
evidence: What do you suppose they said when they reached their homes and found that someone else had been playing jokes, too?
I’m sure I don’t know

readings.title: Little Joe Otter’s Slippery Slide
readings.challenge: Listen for how the fun grows faster and bigger, until it goes wrong for one animal.
readings.focus: A game that is fun for swimmers is dangerous for one who cannot swim, and the teasers become rescuers.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Otters, minks and muskrats swim well and live by the water; real otters do slide down muddy banks for fun. To splutter is to cough and spit out water.
readings.contentNote: As a joke, Billy Mink pushes Peter Rabbit, who cannot swim, into the water; Peter chokes before the others pull him out.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XIV, “Little Joe Otter’s Slippery Slide,” the whole chapter; opens “LITTLE Joe Otter and Billy Mink had been playing together around the Smiling Pool all one…”; closes “…sat down together and watched Little Joe Otter turn a somersault down the slippery slide.”.

questions.prompt: How do Little Joe Otter and his friends make the slide? Show with your hand the ways they go down it.
facilitatorNotes: They find a smooth place on the bank, bring mud and pat it down smooth. They slide on their backs, on their stomachs, head first and feet first.
evidence: brought mud and helped him pat it down smooth
sometimes head first, sometimes feet first

questions.prompt: Peter Rabbit says he left his bathing suit at home. What is the real reason he will not slide?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot swim, and he does not want anyone to know it.
evidence: Now Peter Rabbit couldn’t swim, but he pretended that he didn’t want to.

questions.prompt: Why does everyone laugh when Peter goes splash? Should they be laughing?
facilitatorNotes: Peter is always playing jokes on them, so they enjoy seeing a joke played on him. But he cannot swim, and he is choking. Some children will say it was fair; most will see it stopped being funny.
evidence: for you know Peter Rabbit was forever playing jokes on them
made him choke and splutter

questions.prompt: What does each animal do to save Peter? What does that show about them?
facilitatorNotes: Little Joe Otter takes one ear, Billy Mink the other, Jerry Muskrat carries him on his back and Grandfather Frog swims ahead; the Breezes and Mr. Sun dry him. They tease, but they are friends who help when it matters.
evidence: When Little Joe Otter saw what a dreadful time Peter Rabbit was having he dove into the Smiling Pool

readings.title: The Tale of Tommy Trout Who Didn’t Mind
readings.challenge: Notice that the storyteller tells you how it ends before it happens.
readings.focus: A warning tale: not minding grows, one little speck of a ways at a time, into danger.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Trout are small fish of cool brooks. A pickerel is a long fish with a big mouth that eats smaller fish. To mind someone means to do what they say.
readings.contentNote: A big fish swallows the little trout, and he is never seen again.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XV, “The Tale of Tommy Trout Who Didn’t Mind,” the whole chapter; opens “IN the Laughing Brook, which ripples and sings all day long, lived Mr. Trout and Mrs.…”; closes “And nothing more was ever heard of Tommy Trout, who didn’t mind.”.

questions.prompt: What is the one thing Tommy Trout never could do? How is he different from the other little Trouts?
facilitatorNotes: Mind right away: he always waited a little, and wanted his own way. The others were good and did what Mrs. Trout told them.
evidence: Tommy Trout never could mind right away

questions.prompt: Near the beginning the storyteller says, “there isn’t any Tommy Trout now.” Why tell the ending first?
facilitatorNotes: So listeners hear the rest as a warning and feel worried for him at every step. Some children will say it spoils the story; others that it makes it more exciting. Both are worth hearing.
evidence: there isn’t any Tommy Trout now

questions.prompt: How many times does Tommy swim “just a little speck of a ways”? What does he see each time?
facilitatorNotes: Three times: first he still cannot see around the Big Rock, then he can see almost around it, then he looks right into Mr. Pickerel’s mouth. Each small step seemed safe.
evidence: He swam just a little speck of a ways.
Now he could see almost around the Big Rock.

questions.prompt: The story says Tommy “didn’t mean to be bad.” What do you think the story wants its listeners to learn? Is the ending too hard?
facilitatorNotes: That not minding can be dangerous even when you mean no harm, so a mother’s warning matters. Many children will find the ending very hard for a little fish; that feeling is fair, and it is how warning stories work.
evidence: Tommy Trout didn’t mean to be bad.
He just wanted to have his own way

readings.title: Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race — who is the swiftest?
readings.challenge: Listen for who boasts and who stays calm.
readings.focus: Three boasters agree to settle things with a race, and the slowest animal on the meadow quietly joins it.
readings.context: From Old Mother West Wind, Thornton W. Burgess’s book of animal stories about the Green Meadows. The animals talk and act like people, and the Merry Little Breezes are the wind’s children, a make-believe way of describing the wind. Spotty the Turtle walks very slowly but swims well, as real turtles do. To boast is to brag; a dispute is an argument; the swiftest is the fastest. Hickory and butternut trees grow nuts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race,” from the start to the starting word “Go!”; opens “ALL the little people who lived on the Green Meadows and in the Smiling Pool and along…”; closes ““Are you ready?” asked Grandfather Frog. “Go!””.

questions.prompt: Why is there going to be a race? Who thinks he is the fastest?
facilitatorNotes: Peter Rabbit has been boasting, and Reddy Fox and Billy Mink each think they are faster. Grandfather Frog, who settles arguments, decides a race will tell.
evidence: Peter Rabbit had been boasting of how fast he could run
The best way to decide who is the swiftest is to have a race.

questions.prompt: Tell the plan for the race: where does it start, where do the racers go, and how does someone win?
facilitatorNotes: Start at the old butternut tree, cross the Green Meadows to the little hill, bring back a nut from the big hickory tree; the first one back with a nut wins.
evidence: each bring back a nut from the big hickory which grew there

questions.prompt: Everyone laughs when Peter asks Spotty to race. What does Spotty do?
facilitatorNotes: He does not laugh and does not get cross; he answers with a wise old saying and joins the race.
evidence: but Spotty didn’t laugh and he didn’t get cross because everyone else laughed

questions.prompt: Spotty says the fastest runners do not always get there first. How could a slow turtle win a running race? Look at where he stands at the start.
facilitatorNotes: A prediction. He stands right beside Reddy Fox, which may be a clue. Accept any idea and check it in the next part.
evidence: those who run fastest do not always reach a place first
right side of Reddy Fox Spotty the Turtle

readings.title: Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race — the pond
readings.challenge: Follow each racer’s plan, and the passenger no one notices.
readings.focus: Each runner trusts his own gift, but a hot sun, a pond and a hidden passenger change the race.
readings.context: Recap: Peter Rabbit, Reddy Fox and Billy Mink each said he was the fastest, so Grandfather Frog set a race to fetch a nut from the big hickory tree on the far hill. Everyone laughed when slow Spotty the Turtle joined in. Grandfather Frog has just said “Go!” In dismay means upset and not knowing what to do.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race,” from the start of the race to Spotty climbing out under the hickory tree; opens “Away went Peter Rabbit with great big jumps. After him went Billy Mink so fast that he…”; closes “…saw him. Right across he swam, and climbed up the bank right under the big hickory tree.”.

questions.prompt: How does Spotty the Turtle travel? Why does Reddy Fox never notice?
facilitatorNotes: He grabs the long hair at the end of Reddy’s tail and is carried along. Spotty is light, and Reddy is too excited to feel it.
evidence: Spotty the Turtle reached up and grabbed the long hair on the end of Reddy’s big tail
Reddy Fox was so excited that he did not notice

questions.prompt: Why does Billy Mink slow down? Is it a good plan?
facilitatorNotes: He knows he can swim straight across the pond while the others must run around, so he takes it easy on the hot day. It is clever, but it makes him too sure of himself.
evidence: I will surely get there first.

questions.prompt: What does Mr. Sun do to Peter Rabbit and Reddy Fox?
facilitatorNotes: The more he smiles the hotter it gets; in their thick coats they grow very warm, Peter’s jumps get shorter and Reddy’s tongue hangs out.
evidence: Peter Rabbit had a thick gray coat and Reddy Fox had a thick red coat

questions.prompt: Spotty reaches the hickory tree first. What do you think he will do now?
facilitatorNotes: A prediction: will he grab a nut and go? Something else? Ask the child to remember the guess for tomorrow.
evidence: climbed up the bank right under the big hickory tree

readings.title: Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race — three nuts
readings.challenge: Notice what Spotty does with each of the three nuts.
readings.focus: Patience and a plan win the race, and the boasters lose more than a race.
readings.context: Recap: in the race to fetch a hickory nut, Billy Mink slowed down because he could swim the pond, and Peter Rabbit and Reddy Fox, hot and tired, had to run around it. Spotty the Turtle rode on Reddy’s tail, swam across, and reached the hickory tree first. To accuse is to blame someone; awarded means given the win.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XVI, “Spotty the Turtle Wins a Race,” from the three nuts under the hickory tree to the end of the chapter; opens “Now there were just three nuts left under the hickory tree. Two of these Spotty took down…”; closes “…this day Peter Rabbit and Reddy Fox and Billy Mink can’t bear the sight of a hickory nut.”.

questions.prompt: What does Spotty do with the three nuts? Why hide two of them?
facilitatorNotes: He buries two in the mud at the pond’s edge and carries the third home in his mouth. With the nuts hidden, no one else can bring one back.
evidence: Two of these Spotty took down to the edge of the pond and buried in the mud.

questions.prompt: Why do Peter and Reddy blame Billy Mink? What makes them believe him?
facilitatorNotes: They are hot, tired and cross, and Billy got there before them; but they see how hard he is hunting too.
evidence: they accused Billy Mink of having hidden the nuts
when they saw how hard he was hunting they believed him

questions.prompt: The Merry Little Breezes know who won, but they will not say. Why not?
facilitatorNotes: They want Spotty to show it himself; the surprise is his. Some children will say they are teasing the meadow folk.
evidence: the Merry Little Breezes just laughed and laughed and wouldn’t say a word

questions.prompt: Did Spotty win fairly? Think about the tail ride and the hidden nuts.
facilitatorNotes: The rules said bring back a nut first, and he did, so the meadow folk award him the race. Some children will call riding on Reddy’s tail and hiding nuts a trick; others will call it clever and patient. Ask what Spotty’s wise old saying meant now.
evidence: And so Spotty the Turtle was awarded the race
how he had patiently crawled home
